newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan students take to streets after leader's death.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan students take to streets after leader's death.

text.p: Hundreds of university students marched through the streets of the Kenyan capital on Monday in a second day of protests over the suspected murder of a student leader.
Nairobi University, Kenya's biggest with an estimated 19,000 students, was ordered closed indefinitely by authorities.
Groups of students staged mostly peaceful protests, singing solemn songs in memory of Solomon Muruli who was torn apart by an explosion in his campus bedroom early on Sunday.

"Given the events of recent months, students believe Muruli was murdered," said a student who identified himself only as Leonard. "The explosion ripped his room apart. He was the only fatal victim on the whole floor."
Senior police officers declined comment about Muruli's death and the student protests.
Muruli's room on the sixth floor of Kimberly hostel at Nairobi University's Kikuyu Campus, 30 km (19 miles) from the city centre, was sealed off by police.
The fire that broke out after the explosion in his room gutted an entire wing of the hostel complex.
"We want justice, no more killings," students chanted on Monday as they converged on President Daniel arap Moi's office, national police headquarters and the parliament building.
One group of students screamed "Killers" at riot police.

"In spite of repeated appeals by the university to have students maintain calm during this period of mourning, students in several campuses have taken to the streets lighting fires, hijacking buses and stoning cars," a university statement said.
University spokesman Alfred Mutawali told Reuters Muruli had spoken of death threats and had posted anonymous threats he received on notice boards at his campus.
"We do not know why he was a target, he was a very calm individual," Mutawali said.

Muruli, a fourth year education student, had said he received death threats last week. He said he was kidnapped by police in November after complaining about conditions at the university, beaten and dumped in a churchyard.
Police denied Muruli's allegations.
President Moi sacked Kenya's police commissioner last December after police shot dead two students at Nairobi's Kenyatta University and one student at Egerton University.
A dozen policemen were charged in a court with the deaths at Kenyatta. An inquest is under way in the Egerton case.
The student unrest has come in the run-up to presidential and parliamentary elections due in the next year.

Kenyan students and their leaders have no political agenda, at least in public. Their protests are invariably about issues such as fees, the cost of meals and accommodation and the quality of university administration.
Witnesses said riot police ringed off the main university campus on Monday to forestall riots that started late on Sunday, when students stoned cars on the city's main highway.
The Nairobi Stock Exchange continued business normally.
On Sunday students closed Uhuru highway to traffic for hours by stoning vehicles, ripping down billboards and pulling concrete flower pots into a sidestreet.
